extracted.intended_audience: experimental physicists and scientifically-literate experimenters reproducing or studying photophonic/acoustic effects from intermittent radiant energy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical laboratory protocols and observational criteria for producing and evaluating sounds generated by intermittent radiant (sunlight/artificial light) acting on materials (solids, liquids, gases), including apparatus configurations, materials selection, controls to distinguish mechanisms, and observational precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver design (conical brass cavity with glass plate and hearing-tube)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conical cavity in a piece of brass closed by a flat plate of glass, with a brass tube leading into the cavity serving for connection with the hearing-tube (Fig. 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stuffing the conical cavity with worsted or other fibrous materials produced much louder sounds than a test-tube; smoked wire-gauze placed in the receiver increased loudness. Use the glass lid in position when exposing to intermittent beam; orientation of smoked surface toward the light increases effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material properties for loud sonorous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In solids, the physical condition and the color markedly influence intensity: loudest sounds are produced from substances in a loose, porous, spongy condition, and from those that have the darkest or most absorbent colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best-performing materials include cotton-wool, worsted, fibrous materials generally, cork, sponge, platinum and other metals in a spongy condition, and lampblack. Dark shades (black worsted especially) and smoked/lampblack surfaces give the strongest effects; white cotton-wool performs well among white materials but darkening increases output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lampblack and smoked surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Lampblack (and smoked surfaces) exposed to an intermittent beam of sunlight produce very loud sounds; placing smoked plate-glass with the lampblack surface toward the sun produced sounds audible in any part of the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A teaspoonful of lampblack in a test-tube exposed to intermittent sunlight produced much louder sounds than previously heard; smoke the interior of resonators or test vessels to amplify effects. With smoked surfaces turned away from the light, the sound is much feebler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrupter design for beam modulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two similarly-perforated disks may be employed, one set in rapid rotation while the other remains stationary, to interrupt a beam for producing distant effects without lenses (also usable with artificial light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interrupter produces audible musical signals (like Morse dots and dashes) from sensitive receivers via slight motions of a mirror. For distant work, use a parabolic or conical reflector with a glass vessel containing the sensitive substance placed at the focus; a cylindrical glass vessel may be preferable with a conical reflector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmitter/receiver sizing and distance considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Example given: transmitter diaphragm diameter 5 cm, receiver diameter 5 cm, distance between them 40 metres (about 800 times the diameter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words and sentences spoken into the transmitter in a low tone were audibly reproduced by the lampblack receiver at this distance. For greater distances a heliostat (or means to keep light steadily directed) is necessary. Maintaining steady directed light is critical to remote experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of air cavities when electrically detecting vibration
rubrics_metrics.description: When a telephone is used in circuit with a 'Blake transmitter' carbon button, the wooden box and mouth-piece of the transmitter should be removed so that no air-cavities remain on either side of the diaphragm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precaution prevents confined air-cavity effects and supports detection of real diaphragm vibration by electrical means (telephone, induction coil arrangements). It is used to distinguish diaphragm vibration from effects of confined air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls to distinguish diaphragm vibration vs confined-air effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Design experiments to test whether sonorous effects are due to bending/vibration of plates (Lord Rayleigh's hypothesis) or to expansion/contraction of confined air (Preece's claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (a) Focus beam on hard rubber sheet and listen at portions away from illuminated spot — audibility supports diaphragm vibration. (b) Attach a strip to diaphragm and observe tone; then attach an additional free-centered strip and test — reduction or disappearance of sound except at particular interruption speeds indicates longitudinal expansion/contraction rather than simple pushing force. Use electrical detection (telephone) as an independent check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational procedure for resonator tuning and interruptor speed
rubrics_metrics.description: When the interrupting disk is set rotating then allowed to come gradually to rest, an initial feeble tone is heard that falls in pitch as the interruption rate decreases; minor reinforcements occur more marked as resonator's true pitch is neared; maximum loudness occurs when interruption frequency corresponds to the fundamental frequency of the resonator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen carefully for pitch and loudness changes as rotation slows; minor reinforcements signal approach to resonance. At resonance the sound can be extremely loud (potentially audible to hundreds). Document frequency vs loudness behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquid experiment protocols and precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquids are more difficult to observe; experimental arrangement: fill a very long test-tube with the liquid, slip a flexible rubber tube over the mouth far enough to prevent light reaching the vapor above the surface, prevent reflection from the bottom of the test-tube, and focus an intermittent beam on the middle portion using a large-diameter lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many liquids give no audible sound; those that gave feeble but distinct sounds include sulphuric ether, ammonia, ammonio-sulphate of copper, writing-ink, indigo in sulphuric acid, chloride of copper. Precautions and best circumstances (avoid reflections, prevent light on vapor) are required; transmitting vibrations to the ear via a solid rod may improve detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaseous/vapor sonorousness and selection of vapors
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain vapors are highly sonorous under an intermittent beam: water-vapor, coal-gas, sulphuric ether, alcohol, ammonia, amylene, ethyl bromide, diethylamine, mercury, iodine, and peroxide of nitrogen; iodine and peroxide of nitrogen gave the loudest sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Tyndall's suggestion to compare vapors of different heat-absorbent properties (e.g., sulphuric ether vs bisulphide of carbon) — better absorbers yield louder sounds. Repeat and verify across vapors; safety caution implied when using reactive/toxic vapors (iodine, peroxide of nitrogen, mercury).

rubrics_metrics.name: General experimental standard: test across physical states and repeatability
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds are produced by intermittent sunlight from substances in every physical condition (solid, liquid, gaseous); investigators should test broadly and repeat experiments to verify results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep records of prior experiments for comparison (e.g., earlier mica diaphragm tests); repeat earlier setups (smoked mica, smoked diaphragms) under similar and improved conditions. Note that some substances initially reported non-responsive later yielded sounds under more careful conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesized mechanism: heating-driven expansion/contraction of porous materials
rubrics_metrics.description: For lampblack and similar porous materials: particles heated by rays expand, contracting the air-spaces among them and expelling a pulse of air; cooling enlarges air-spaces and draws in outside air, producing waves of condensation and rarefaction in the atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sponge/air-space model to interpret why lampblack produces intense airborne vibrations while communicating little vibration to the solid substrate. Consider both particle heating and heating of entrained air when selecting materials and predicting acoustic output.
